title: Bearing capacity and foundation settlements
summary: Two things must be right to score reliably here. First, keep the four bearing-capacity terms apart — gross, net, ultimate, safe, allowable — because most wrong answers come from mixing gross and net rather than from the theory. Second, remember that allowable bearing pressure is the LESSER of the shear-governed and settlement-governed values, and that which one governs depends on the soil: settlement in sand, shear in soft clay. Terzaghi's three-term equation and the local-shear reduction factors are the standard computations.

sections.heading: Modes of failure and Terzaghi's theory
sections.body:
**Three modes of bearing failure**, distinguished by the soil's density or stiffness:

| Mode | Occurs in | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **General shear** | **Dense sand, stiff clay** | A well-defined failure surface reaches the ground surface; **heave** beside the footing; a **sudden, catastrophic** failure with a clear peak load |
| **Local shear** | **Medium dense sand, medium clay** | Failure surface only partly developed; some heave; no clear peak |
| **Punching shear** | **Very loose sand, very soft clay** | The footing simply **punches down**; no heave, no failure surface reaching the surface |

The practical significance: **general shear gives warning through a clear peak load**, whereas punching failure is a progressive settlement with no identifiable ultimate load — so the design criterion for very loose soil becomes settlement rather than capacity.

**Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation** for a **strip** footing:

> **q_u = c N_c + γ D_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ**

The three terms have distinct physical meanings, and understanding them makes the equation memorable:

| Term | Contribution from |
|---|---|
| **c N_c** | **Cohesion** of the soil |
| **γ D_f N_q** | **Surcharge** — the weight of soil above founding level |
| **0.5 γ B N_γ** | **Self-weight of the soil in the failure wedge**, hence the **width** of the footing |

Two consequences follow immediately, and both are examinable:

- For a **pure clay (φ = 0)**, N_q = 1 and **N_γ = 0**, so **q_u = c N_c + γD_f** with **N_c = 5.7** (Terzaghi) or **5.14** (Prandtl/Vesic). The **width does not appear** — bearing capacity in clay is **independent of footing width**.
- For a **pure sand (c = 0)**, the first term vanishes and capacity **grows with both depth and width**.

That contrast explains a great deal of practice: widening a footing on clay does not increase the bearing *pressure* it can take (only the total load), while on sand it does.

**Shape factors** convert the strip result to real footings (IS 6403):

| Shape | Correction |
|---|---|
| Strip | 1.0 (the base case) |
| **Square** | N_c × 1.3, N_γ × 0.8 |
| **Circular** | N_c × 1.3, N_γ × 0.6 |
| **Rectangular** | N_c(1 + 0.2B/L), N_γ(1 − 0.2B/L) |

**Local shear reduction.** Where local shear governs, use reduced parameters:

> **c′ = ⅔ c**  and  **tan φ′ = ⅔ tan φ**

**Water table correction.** A high water table reduces capacity, because the **effective** unit weight in the failure zone falls from γ to γ′ ≈ γ/2. Applied through factors **R_w1** (on the surcharge term) and **R_w2** (on the width term), each ranging from **0.5** when the water table is at or above founding level to **1.0** when it is more than B below the base. **A rising water table can nearly halve the bearing capacity of a sand** — a point worth remembering for the Terai and the Kathmandu Valley.

**Other theories**, offered as distractors and occasionally asked directly: **Prandtl** (plasticity solution, the origin of N_c = 5.14), **Meyerhof** (a more complete failure surface, with depth and inclination factors), **Skempton** (for clays, N_c varying with D/B), **Hansen** and **Vesic** (general equations with factors for shape, depth, inclination and ground slope), and **IS 6403**, which is what Nepali and Indian practice follows.

sections.heading: Gross, net, safe and allowable — keeping them apart
sections.body:
This is where most marks are lost, and the distinction is bookkeeping rather than theory.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Gross pressure** | The **total** pressure at founding level, **including** the weight of soil previously there |
| **Net pressure** | The **increase** over the original overburden: **q_net = q_gross − γD_f** |
| **Ultimate bearing capacity q_u** | The **gross** pressure at which shear failure occurs |
| **Net ultimate q_nu** | **q_u − γD_f** |
| **Net safe bearing capacity** | **q_nu / F**, with **F = 2.5 or 3** |
| **Safe bearing capacity (gross)** | q_nu/F **+ γD_f** |
| **Allowable bearing pressure** | The **LESSER** of the safe bearing capacity and the pressure limited by **settlement** |

**The key relationships:**

> **q_nu = q_u − γ D_f**
> **q_ns = q_nu / F**
> **q_safe (gross) = q_nu/F + γ D_f**

**Note that the factor of safety is applied to the NET value, not the gross.** The reason is physical: the overburden pressure γD_f was already there before construction and the soil has long carried it, so it needs no factor of safety. Applying F to the gross value is over-conservative and is a genuine error, not merely a convention.

**Allowable bearing pressure is the lesser of two quite different limits**, and which one governs depends on the soil:

| Soil | Usually governed by | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Dense sand and gravel** | **Settlement** | Shear capacity is ample; settlement is immediate and can be excessive under a wide footing |
| **Soft to medium clay** | **Shear (bearing capacity)** | Capacity is low; and settlement, though large, occurs over years |
| Stiff clay | Either | Both must be checked |
| Rock | Neither, usually | Capacity vastly exceeds requirement |

Assuming that shear always governs is one of the commonest conceptual errors in foundation design, and it is why **presumptive bearing values** in codes are hedged with warnings.

**Presumptive (safe) bearing capacities** from IS 1904, for preliminary sizing only:

| Soil / rock | Presumptive value (kN/m²) |
|---|---|
| Hard rock | 3300 and above |
| Soft rock | 440 |
| **Gravel, dense sand** | **440** |
| Medium sand | 245 |
| **Loose sand** | **100** |
| Hard / stiff clay | 440 / 245 |
| **Soft clay** | **100** |
| Very soft clay, peat | **50 or to be determined** |

These are **presumptive** — they must never be used for a final design where a site investigation is possible, because they take no account of the footing width, depth, water table or settlement.

**Determining bearing capacity in practice:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Analytical** (Terzaghi, IS 6403) | From c and φ obtained by testing |
| **Plate load test** | Direct, but a **shallow** pressure bulb — good for sand, misleading for clay |
| **SPT correlations** | Rapid, widely used for sand |
| **CPT correlations** | A continuous profile |
| Presumptive values | Preliminary only |

sections.heading: Settlement
sections.body:
> **Total settlement = immediate (elastic) + primary consolidation + secondary compression**

| Component | Dominant in | Timescale |
|---|---|---|
| **Immediate (elastic)** | **Sand and gravel** | Essentially **during construction** |
| **Primary consolidation** | **Saturated clay** | **Months to years** |
| **Secondary compression** | Organic and highly plastic soils | Years to decades |

So in **sand** settlement is effectively **complete by the end of construction**, while in **clay** most of it is still to come — which decides which analysis is needed and when damage will appear.

**Immediate settlement:**

> **S_i = q B (1 − μ²) I_f / E_s**

**Consolidation settlement:**

> **S_c = (C_c H/(1 + e_0)) · log₁₀[(σ′_0 + Δσ)/σ′_0]**

Note the **logarithm**: the same stress increment causes far less settlement at depth, where σ′_0 is already large, than near the surface.

**For an over-consolidated clay** the settlement is computed on the flat **recompression** index C_r while σ′_0 + Δσ remains below the preconsolidation pressure σ′_c, switching to C_c beyond it. Recognising over-consolidation can reduce a settlement estimate by an order of magnitude, which is why **Casagrande's construction** for σ′_c is worth doing carefully.

**Permissible settlements (IS 1904):**

| Structure and soil | Maximum total settlement |
|---|---|
| **Isolated footing on sand** | **40 mm** |
| **Isolated footing on clay** | **65 mm** |
| **Raft on sand** | **40 – 65 mm** |
| **Raft on clay** | **65 – 100 mm** |

Clay is allowed more because the settlement occurs **slowly**, so the structure can accommodate it by creep and progressive adjustment rather than being strained suddenly.

**Differential settlement matters far more than total.** A building settling **50 mm uniformly** is undamaged — services and approaches need adjusting, nothing more. A building settling **10 mm unevenly** cracks. The governing measure is the **angular distortion δ/L**:

| Angular distortion | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1/500** | Safe limit for buildings where cracking is not permissible |
| **1/300** | Cracking of panel walls begins |
| 1/250 | Structural damage to be expected |
| 1/150 | Considerable cracking; tilting visible |

**Causes of differential settlement**, and each has a design response:

| Cause | Response |
|---|---|
| **Non-uniform soil** across the site | Proportion footings for **equal settlement**, not equal pressure |
| **Unequal column loads** on equal footings | Same |
| **Varying footing depths** | Keep founding level consistent where possible |
| **Local variation in water table** | Investigate adequately |
| Non-uniform load history (an extension to an old building) | Separate the new work with a **movement joint** |

**Reducing settlement**, in order of usual preference: **increase the depth** (mobilising stronger soil and reducing net pressure), **increase the area** (reducing pressure), use a **raft** to tie the structure together, use **piles** to reach a firmer stratum, **improve the ground** (compaction, stone columns, preloading, sand drains), or **design the structure to tolerate** the movement (a jointed or flexible frame).

**Preloading with vertical drains** is the elegant option for a large area of soft clay: a surcharge is placed to induce most of the settlement **before** construction, and **sand or prefabricated vertical drains** shorten the drainage path so it happens in months rather than decades. The drains do not change **how much** settlement occurs — only **how fast**, because **T_v = c_v t/d²** makes time vary as the **square** of the drainage path.

**A closing caution on parameters.** Bearing capacity and settlement calculations are only as good as c, φ, E_s and c_v, which are measured on small specimens of a variable material. Two significant figures is generous precision. The professional response is to bracket the answer with sensible ranges, choose conservatively where the consequence of error is severe, and — where the structure is important — verify by **plate load test, pile load test or instrumented monitoring** rather than trusting the arithmetic alone.

formulas.label: Terzaghi bearing capacity (strip footing)
formulas.expression: q_u = c N_c + γ D_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ
formulas.note: For φ = 0: N_γ = 0, N_q = 1, N_c = 5.7 — so capacity in clay is INDEPENDENT of footing width.

formulas.label: Net and safe bearing capacity
formulas.expression: q_nu = q_u − γD_f ;   q_ns = q_nu/F ;   q_safe(gross) = q_nu/F + γD_f
formulas.note: The factor of safety applies to the NET value, because the overburden was already carried by the soil.

formulas.label: Allowable bearing pressure
formulas.expression: q_allowable = LESSER of (safe bearing capacity) and (pressure limited by settlement)
formulas.note: Settlement usually governs on dense sand; shear usually governs on soft clay.

formulas.label: Local shear reduction
formulas.expression: c′ = ⅔c ;   tan φ′ = ⅔ tan φ
formulas.note: Applied where local shear governs — medium dense sand, medium clay.

formulas.label: Shape factors (IS 6403)
formulas.expression: Square: N_c × 1.3, N_γ × 0.8.  Circular: N_c × 1.3, N_γ × 0.6.  Rectangular: N_c(1+0.2B/L), N_γ(1−0.2B/L)
formulas.note: The strip footing is the base case from which all others are corrected.

formulas.label: Immediate settlement
formulas.expression: S_i = q B (1 − μ²) I_f / E_s
formulas.note: Dominates in sand and gravel, and is essentially complete by the end of construction.

formulas.label: Consolidation settlement
formulas.note: Use C_r instead of C_c while below the preconsolidation pressure σ′_c.

formulas.label: Angular distortion limit
formulas.expression: δ/L ≤ 1/500 where cracking is not permissible;  cracking begins about 1/300
formulas.note: Differential settlement, not total, is what damages a structure.

formulas.label: Time factor and vertical drains
formulas.note: Drains shorten d, so time falls as its square — they change how FAST, not how MUCH.
